title: Clinical and Omics Data Visualization in R
text:
Preface
cliomicplot produces publication-ready clinical and multi-omics figures in R with a formula grammar and pre-configured journal styles. This handbook explains how to use the package for clinical trial reporting, high-dimensional omics profiling, systems biology network coupling, and multi-panel journal composite assembly conforming to international publication specifications.

title: Clinical and Omics Data Visualization in R
text:
About This Handbook
Biomedical data science routinely requires visualizing disparate data modalities—ranging from patient survival times and longitudinal biomarker trajectories to transcriptomic differential expression profiles and complex coupled molecular networks. Standard visualization libraries frequently require dozens of boilerplate lines for basic journal conventions: risk tables aligned below Kaplan-Meier survival curves, statistical significance callouts, outward tick marks, uppercase panel labels, and color-blind safe palettes.
cliomicplot unifies these workflows under an expressive formula interface:
\text{response} \sim \text{predictor} \mid \text{grouping}
By pairing this formula syntax with pre-built journal themes (theme_cli_nature(), theme_cli_lancet(), theme_cli_nejm(), theme_cli_cell()), researchers can move from raw data to peer-review ready figures in a single function call.

Core Design Philosophy: Every plot type in cliomicplot adheres to rigorous graphic standards—open L-frame axes, outward tick marks, CIEDE2000-separated palettes, and automated layout alignment.

text:
Visual Grammar & Mental Models
Throughout this handbook, visualizations are structured around five core patterns:

The Formula Interface: A single consistent calling convention cliplot(y ~ x, data = df, type = type_*) across univariate, bivariate, survival, network, and meta-analytic figures.
Journal Style Presets: Automated formatting rules conforming to publication guidelines for Nature, The Lancet, NEJM, Cell, JAMA, and Science.
Multi-Layer Alignment: Seamless integration of risk tables, difference bars, forest subgroup annotations, and benchmark bars without manual coordinate math.
Coupled Network Topology: Spatial positioning of molecular and microbial networks coupled with peripheral environmental heatmaps and triangular Mantel links.
Reproducible Case Studies: Full-scale reproductions of figures from high-impact literature (Nature Communications, Nature Metabolism, Lancet Oncology, JACI).

Handbook Structure
The handbook is organized into five thematic parts:

Part I — Graphic Grammar and Design System (Chapters 1–2): The unified cliplot() formula syntax, theme resolvers, and journal styling presets conforming to AI4SciFig publication gates.
Part II — Clinical Trials and Survival Analysis (Chapters 3–6): Time-to-event curves with risk tables, subgroup treatment effects, oncology response tracking (RECIST waterfall and swimmer plots), and minimally clinically important difference (MCID) modeling.
Part III — High-Dimensional Omics Visualizations (Chapters 7–10): Volcano plots with biomarker callout boxes, pathway enrichment running scores, microbiome GWAS Manhattan architectures, and taxonomic dyad sharing.
Part IV — Systems Biology and Coupled Multi-Network Architectures (Chapters 11–15): Cross-network module overlap (RF, Jaccard), multi-group network layouts across 10 journal styles, modular polygon rings (PolygonRrClusterG), transkingdom bipartite networks, triangular environmental Mantel links, Zi-Pi keystone hub classification, ecological edge-sign dynamics, module preservation, and permutation testing.
Part V — Publication Composites and Applied Case Studies (Chapters 16–24): Figure assembly with patchwork and full-scale reproducible workflows for atopic dermatitis, immuno-oncology, nasal polyps (Nature Communications), deconvolution identifiability, network meta-analysis, and nanoplastics multi-omics audit (Nature Metabolism).

1.1 Formula Syntax
cliplot() provides a single entry point for generating biomedical visualizations through a formula syntax. This chapter details the formula grammar, the parameter system (clipar), and the type dispatch architecture.
cliplot() accepts standard R formulas mapping variables to visual roles:

y ~ x: Bivariate plots (boxplots, scatter plots, violin plots, ROC curves).
y ~ x | facet: Conditioned plots faceted across biological subgroups or clinical trial cohorts.
Surv(time, event) ~ arm: Time-to-event outcomes with survival curves, risk tables, and hazard ratios.
~ x: Univariate distributions (histograms, density estimates, rank-abundance curves).

# General syntax
p <- cliplot(
  formula = Value ~ Biomarker,
  data    = clinical_data,
  type    = "boxplot",
  preset  = "nature"
)

1.2 Function Dispatch and Plot Types
The type argument selects the geometry and statistical layer. It accepts either character aliases or typed constructor functions:


Show R code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)

# Generate reproducible clinical cohort
set.seed(42)
df_cohort <- data.frame(
  Biomarker  = factor(rep(c("Control", "Mild_AD", "Severe_AD"), each = 40),
                      levels = c("Control", "Mild_AD", "Severe_AD")),
  Treatment  = factor(rep(rep(c("Placebo", "Biologic"), each = 20), 3),
                      levels = c("Placebo", "Biologic")),
  Age_Group  = factor(rep(c("Pediatric", "Adult"), 60)),
  IL13_pg_ml = c(
    rnorm(20, 5.2, 0.9), rnorm(20, 3.8, 0.8),
    rnorm(20, 10.5, 1.4), rnorm(20, 7.2, 1.2),
    rnorm(20, 18.2, 2.1), rnorm(20, 11.5, 1.8)
  )
)

# Direct character specification
p_box <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker,
  data   = df_cohort,
  type   = "boxplot",
  preset = "nature",
  title  = "Serum IL-13 by Clinical Severity"
)
p_box










1.2.1 Typed Constructor Functions
Constructor functions configure geometry-specific options with autocomplete support:


Show R code
p_viol <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker,
  data  = df_cohort,
  type  = type_violin(inner = "boxplot", trim = FALSE),
  theme = "lancet"
)
p_viol

1.3 The 4-Step Progressive Pipeline: Basic, Color, Template, and Statistics
Scientific figures in cliomicplot are constructed through a four-step layered workflow: geometry baseline, palette coloring, journal templating, and statistical testing with comparison bars.

1.3.1 Step 1: The Basic Geometry
A single formula call renders the unadorned baseline geometry using default styling:


Show R code
p_step1 <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker,
  data = df_cohort,
  type = "violin"
)
p_step1











1.3.2 Step 2: Add Curated Scientific Color
Applying a publication palette (palette = "nature") assigns coordinated categorical hues across experimental cohorts:


Show R code
p_step2 <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker,
  data    = df_cohort,
  type    = "violin",
  palette = "nature"
)
p_step2











1.3.3 Step 3: Add Journal Template and Typography
Applying a journal template (theme = "nature") configures open axes, tick direction, typography, panel titles, and axis labels:


Show R code
p_step3 <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker,
  data     = df_cohort,
  type     = type_violin(inner = "quartiles", quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)),
  palette  = "nature",
  theme    = "nature",
  title    = "Serum IL-13 by Clinical Severity Tier",
  subtitle = "Nature template with interior quartile contours (25%, median, 75%)",
  ylab     = "Serum IL-13 (pg/mL)",
  xlab     = "Biomarker Severity Tier"
)
p_step3











1.3.4 Step 4: Add Statistical Hypothesis Testing with Comparison Bars
Setting stat.test = "wilcox.test" calculates non-parametric rank-sum statistics and draws comparison bracket bars across cohorts:


Show R code
p_step4 <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker,
  data      = df_cohort,
  type      = type_violin(inner = "boxplot", add_jitter = TRUE, jitter_alpha = 0.35),
  palette   = "nature",
  theme     = "nature",
  stat.test = "wilcox.test",
  title     = "Serum IL-13 Across Clinical Severity Stages",
  subtitle  = "Pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum test with comparison bracket bars",
  ylab      = "Serum IL-13 (pg/mL)",
  xlab      = "Biomarker Severity Tier"
)
p_step4

1.4 Advanced Distribution Architectures: Split Violins and Rainclouds
cliomicplot provides specialized distribution types for multi-arm clinical trials and single-cell cohorts.

1.4.1 Dual-Condition Contrast: type_split_violin()
When comparing two treatment arms (Placebo vs. Biologic) across multiple severity tiers, type_split_violin() renders both distributions back-to-back along a shared category spine. Each condition is highlighted by group color, with inner boxplots dodged inside each split half. Adding stat.test = "t.test" performs within-tier comparisons with horizontal bracket bars:


Show R code
p_split <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker | Treatment,
  data      = df_cohort,
  type      = type_split_violin(
    inner     = "boxplot",
    scale     = "width"
  ),
  palette   = "jco",
  theme     = "scifig",
  stat.test = "t.test",
  title     = "IL-13 Modulation Under Biologic vs. Placebo Across Severity Tiers",
  subtitle  = "Split-half comparison with within-tier two-sample t-test",
  ylab      = "Serum IL-13 (pg/mL)",
  xlab      = "Biomarker Severity Tier"
)
p_split











1.4.2 Mean Diamond Glyphs with Standard Error: inner = "mean_se"
Setting inner = "mean_se" replaces median boxplots with an arithmetic mean diamond and standard error errorbars:


Show R code
p_mean_stat <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Treatment,
  data      = df_cohort,
  by        = "Treatment",
  type      = type_violin(
    inner        = "mean_se",
    add_jitter   = TRUE,
    jitter_width = 0.12,
    jitter_alpha = 0.40,
    jitter_size  = 1.6
  ),
  palette   = "cell",
  legend    = "none",
  stat.test = "wilcox.test",
  title     = "Biologic Efficacy on Circulating IL-13",
  subtitle  = "Violin density with raw observations, mean ± SEM diamond, and Wilcoxon test",
  ylab      = "Serum IL-13 (pg/mL)"
)

text:
1.5 Nature Aging Pathology Boxplots: type_pathology_boxplot()
type_pathology_boxplot() implements the Nature Aging and SciFig boxplot standard established in Yadav et al. 2026. Designed for large-cohort clinical and multi-tissue omics contrasts (such as GTEx donors stratified by microscopic pathology findings), it incorporates seven publication elements:

Category-matched colored outlines: Box outlines and whiskers match the group palette (#0F4D92 vs. #D55E00), while box interiors retain low-alpha fill (alpha = 0.22).
Bold black median bar: An explicit #111111 horizontal crossbar (linewidth = 0.85) highlights the sample median without obscuring point distributions.
Paired mean connecting lines: Dotted trajectories connect group means across conditions within each category, showing effect direction.
Mean diamond glyphs: A white-filled diamond marker (shape = 23) displays the arithmetic mean.
Dashed zero baseline: A horizontal reference line (y = 0) renders behind all distributions.
Subsampled jitter: jitter_subsample downsamples massive background groups (e.g. N \approx 20\text{k}) to prevent overplotting while keeping box statistics computed on all observations.
Mathematical significance brackets: stat.label = "p.nature" renders two-line significance annotations with exact Unicode scientific exponents (***\text{ (P = }1.7 \times 10^{-9}\text{)} or \text{n.s. (P = 0.55)}).



Show R code
# Simulate multi-tissue pathology data
set.seed(42)
pathology_df <- data.frame(
  feature = factor(rep(c("Calcification\n(n = 225)", "Fibrosis\n(n = 531)", "Atrophy\n(n = 301)"), each = 80)),
  status  = factor(rep(c("Absent (~20k)", "Present"), each = 40, times = 3), levels = c("Absent (~20k)", "Present")),
  delta   = c(
    rnorm(40, mean = 0.10, sd = 0.07), rnorm(40, mean = 0.13, sd = 0.08),
    rnorm(40, mean = 0.13, sd = 0.08), rnorm(40, mean = 0.16, sd = 0.09),
    rnorm(40, mean = 0.13, sd = 0.08), rnorm(40, mean = 0.14, sd = 0.14)
  )
)

p_pathology <- cliplot(
  delta ~ feature | status,
  data       = pathology_df,
  type       = type_pathology_boxplot(
    width            = 0.30,
    position_dodge   = 0.42,
    alpha            = 0.22,
    linewidth        = 0.45,
    jitter_subsample = 40,
    jitter_size      = 0.85,
    jitter_alpha     = 0.35,
    mean_size        = 1.8,
    bold_median_lwd  = 0.85
  ),
  palette    = "pathology",
  theme      = "pathology",
  stat.test  = "t.test",
  stat.label = "p.nature",
  stat.y     = c(0.38, 0.42, 0.48),
  title      = "Structural Aging Across Microscopic Pathology Findings",
  subtitle   = "Nature Aging boxplot architecture with paired mean trajectory lines",
  xlab       = "Microscopic Pathology Finding",
  ylab       = "Structural Aging Δ Score"
)
p_pathology

1.6 Ecology & Demographic Viability Rainclouds: type_ecology_raincloud()
In ecology, evolutionary demographics, and population viability analyses, distributions are often visualized using half-boxed raincloud composites. type_ecology_raincloud() (alias type_half_boxed()) implements this architecture with six components:

White-filled boxplot with colored outline: A vertical boxplot nudged to the left (box_nudge = -0.15, width = 0.17) with solid white fill (#FFFFFF), thick category-colored borders (linewidth = 1.1), and open square outlier markers (shape = 0, size = 2.0).
Central mean dot: A solid circular marker (shape = 16, size = 3.8) positioned directly between the boxplot and the violin density.
Right-facing half-violin density: A density slab (ggdist::stat_halfeye or base R fallback) extending rightward from a flat vertical spine.
Reference baseline: A dashed horizontal line (e.g. ref_line = 1.0 representing demographic population replacement equilibrium \lambda = 1.0).
Mean and 95% CI text annotation: Automated Student’s t 95% Confidence Interval calculation rendered directly below each category: \lambda = \bar{y}, \quad (95\%\text{ CI: } \bar{y} \pm t_{n-1, 0.975} \times \text{SE})
Ecology theme: theme = "ecology" establishes a 4-sided rectangular border, clean white interior, outward ticks, and bold axis typography.



Show R code
# Simulate reseeding viability data (population growth rate lambda across years)
set.seed(42)
n_reps <- 250
y_2yr  <- rnorm(n_reps, mean = 0.869, sd = 0.055)
y_5yr  <- rnorm(n_reps, mean = 0.713, sd = 0.042)
y_10yr <- rnorm(n_reps, mean = 0.727, sd = 0.045)
# Add outlier replicates matching open square glyphs
y_2yr[1:4]  <- c(1.03, 1.05, 0.72, 0.71)
y_5yr[1:3]  <- c(0.85, 0.60, 0.59)
y_10yr[1:3] <- c(0.86, 0.84, 0.60)

reseeding_df <- data.frame(
  years = factor(rep(c("2 yr", "5 yr", "10 yr"), each = n_reps), levels = c("2 yr", "5 yr", "10 yr")),
  growth_rate = c(y_2yr, y_5yr, y_10yr)
)

p_ecology <- cliplot(
  growth_rate ~ years,
  data       = reseeding_df,
  type       = type_ecology_raincloud(
    ref_line       = 1.0,
    show_stats     = TRUE,
    stat_param     = "\u03bb",
    stat_digits    = 3,
    stat_y_pos     = 0.52
  ),
  palette    = "ecology",
  theme      = "ecology",
  xlab       = "Reseeding years",
  ylab       = expression(paste("population growth rate (", lambda, ")"))
) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0.48, 1.11),
    breaks = seq(0.5, 1.1, by = 0.1)
  )
p_ecology

section: 1.7 Transparent Data Distribution: Scatter-Box-Violin Plots (David Baranger Style)
text:
1.7 Transparent Data Distribution: Scatter-Box-Violin Plots (David Baranger Style)
A recognized issue in biomedical and behavioral data visualization is the over-reliance on bar plots with standard error bars (“dynamite plungers”), which obscure sample sizes, bimodal clusters, skewness, and outliers. In “Showing your data: Scatter, box, & violin plots” (2018), David Baranger advocates layering three complementary representations of the data:

Background Kernel Density (geom_violin): Shows the overall probability density and distribution shape (alpha = 0.30, scale = "width", linewidth = 0.55).
Foreground Notched Boxplot (geom_boxplot): A narrow summary structure (width = 0.22, alpha = 0.75) with black borders and notches indicating the 95% confidence interval of the median (1.58 \times \text{IQR} / \sqrt{n}). Outliers are hidden (outlier.shape = NA) to eliminate duplicate points.
Overlaid Raw Data Points (geom_jitter / geom_point): Individual observations displayed with black borders (shape = 21, stroke = 0.35, size = 1.8, alpha = 0.65) and fill colors matching the treatment category, ensuring complete transparency.

cliomicplot provides type_scatter_box_violin() (aliases: type_baranger(), type_sbv(), and type_boxplot(style = "baranger")), as well as two-component variants type_scatter_box() and type_box_violin().

1.7.1 Single-Factor Demonstration


Show R code
p_sbv_single <- cliplot(
  Sepal.Length ~ Species,
  data     = iris,
  type     = type_scatter_box_violin(notch = TRUE),
  palette  = "nature",
  theme    = "nature",
  title    = "Fisher Iris Sepal Length Distribution",
  subtitle = "David Baranger scatter-box-violin architecture with 95% median CI notches",
  ylab     = "Sepal Length (cm)",
  xlab     = "Iris Species"
)
p_sbv_single











1.7.2 Dodged 2-Way Grouping Demonstration
When conditioning on a secondary treatment or demographic factor (y ~ x | group), type_scatter_box_violin() automatically coordinates synchronized dodging across all three visual layers using position_dodge(0.80) and position_jitterdodge(0.12, 0.80):


Show R code
tg <- ToothGrowth
tg$dose <- factor(tg$dose, levels = c(0.5, 1.0, 2.0), labels = c("0.5 mg/day", "1.0 mg/day", "2.0 mg/day"))

p_sbv_grouped <- cliplot(
  len ~ dose | supp,
  data     = tg,
  type     = type_scatter_box_violin(notch = FALSE, width = 0.20, position_dodge = 0.80),
  palette  = "jco",
  theme    = "nature",
  title    = "Odontoblast Growth by Ascorbic Acid Regimen and Delivery Vehicle",
  subtitle = "Synchronized 2-way dodging across violin, notched box, and raw observation points",
  ylab     = "Tooth Length",
  xlab     = "Dose Level"
)
p_sbv_grouped

2.2 Side-by-Side Journal Theme Comparison on Proteomics Data
Using the bundled cortex proteomics dataset (ADPD_cortex_Maxquant.RData), we compare biomarker abundances across four journal presets:


Show R code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Load bundled AD/PD cortex proteomics data
data_path <- system.file("extdata", "ADPD_cortex_Maxquant.RData", package = "cliomicplot")
e_adpd <- new.env()
load(data_path, envir = e_adpd)
adpd_res <- e_adpd$results_long

# Filter Alzheimer's vs Control contrast
sub_res <- as.data.frame(adpd_res[adpd_res$test == "ADvsCTL" & !is.na(adpd_res$P.Value), ])
sub_res$pValue <- sub_res$P.Value

# 1. Nature style (open axes, slate blue / crimson palette)
p_nat <- cliplot(-log10(pValue) ~ logFC, data = sub_res,
                 type   = type_volcano(fc_cutoff = 0.5, pval_cutoff = 0.05),
                 preset = "nature", title = "Nature Style")

# 2. Science style (jewel tones, high contrast)
p_sci <- cliplot(-log10(pValue) ~ logFC, data = sub_res,
                 type   = type_volcano(fc_cutoff = 0.5, pval_cutoff = 0.05),
                 preset = "science", title = "Science Style")

# 3. Cell style (structured frame, vivid accents)
p_cel <- cliplot(-log10(pValue) ~ logFC, data = sub_res,
                 type   = type_volcano(fc_cutoff = 0.5, pval_cutoff = 0.05),
                 preset = "cell", title = "Cell Style")

# 4. Lancet style (minimalist editorial grey, thin strokes)
p_lan <- cliplot(-log10(pValue) ~ logFC, data = sub_res,
                 type   = type_volcano(fc_cutoff = 0.5, pval_cutoff = 0.05),
                 preset = "lancet", title = "Lancet Style")

(p_nat | p_sci) / (p_cel | p_lan)

title: 3  Survival Analysis and Time-to-Event Graphics
text:
3.1 Kaplan-Meier Curves: type = "km"
Time-to-event outcomes require specialized visual conventions. cliplot() implements Kaplan-Meier survival curves with aligned risk tables and Fine-Gray cumulative incidence curves for competing risks.
cliplot(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, data, type = "km") estimates the step survival function \hat{S}(t):
\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_i \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right)
where d_i is the number of events and n_i is the number of individuals at risk at time t_i.

title: 3  Survival Analysis and Time-to-Event Graphics
text:
3.1.1 Overall Survival with Landmark Milestones (NEJM Style)
Reporting overall survival (OS) requires both the step survival function and explicit landmark milestone rates (e.g., 6-month, 1-year, and 2-year survival) with confidence intervals.


Show R code
library(cliomicplot)
library(survival)
library(ggplot2)

clitheme("nejm")

p_km <- cliplot(
  Surv(time, status) ~ sex,
  data = lung,
  type = type_km(
    risk_table  = TRUE,
    pval        = TRUE,
    conf_int    = TRUE,
    median_line = TRUE,
    milestones  = c(180, 365, 730)
  ),
  palette  = "nejm",
  title    = "Overall Survival Stratified by Sex",
  subtitle = "NCCTG Lung Cancer Trial (n = 228) with 6-mo, 1-yr, 2-yr Milestones",
  xlab     = "Time on Study (days)",
  ylab     = "Survival Probability",
  legend   = "top"
)
p_km









Key features of type_km(): - Landmark milestones annotated directly on curves with percentage estimates and error bars. - Aligned numbers-at-risk table matching x-axis tick positions. - Dashed drop lines indicating median survival time for each cohort.

text:
4.1 The Forest Plot Grammar: type = "forest"
Forest plots summarize treatment effects and evaluate consistency across patient subgroups in randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses. cliomicplot formats forest plots with tabular columns, logarithmic axes, and summary diamonds.
In clinical studies, treatment effect sizes (Hazard Ratios \text{HR}, Odds Ratios \text{OR}, or Relative Risks \text{RR}) are displayed on a logarithmic scale with 95% confidence intervals:
\log(\widehat{\text{HR}}) \pm 1.96 \times \text{SE}(\log(\widehat{\text{HR}}))

text:
4.1.1 Multivariable Cox Proportional Hazards Model (Science Style)
We fit a multivariable Cox model directly to the NCCTG lung cancer cohort (survival::lung), estimating independent hazard ratios for age, sex, ECOG performance status, and weight loss:


Show R code
library(cliomicplot)
library(survival)
library(ggplot2)

# Fit Cox proportional hazards model
cox_fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog + wt.loss, data = lung)
cox_sum <- summary(cox_fit)

# Prepare forest plot data frame
forest_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("Age (per year)", "Male vs. Female",
               "ECOG PS (per point)", "Weight loss (per lb)"),
  HR       = cox_sum$conf.int[, "exp(coef)"],
  CI_low   = cox_sum$conf.int[, "lower .95"],
  CI_high  = cox_sum$conf.int[, "upper .95"],
  P        = cox_sum$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

clitheme("science")

p_forest_cox <- cliplot(
  HR ~ Variable,
  data = forest_df,
  type = type_forest(
    ref_line    = TRUE,
    ref_val     = 1.0,
    sort        = TRUE,
    point_size  = 3.5,
    ci_width    = 1.0,
    stripe      = TRUE,
    show_values = TRUE,
    sig_color   = "#E64B35",
    ns_color    = "#3C5488"
  ),
  title    = "Multivariable Cox Proportional Hazards Model",
  subtitle = "Overall Survival Hazard Ratios (95% CI) with Zebra Row Stripes",
  caption  = "NCCTG Advanced Lung Cancer (n = 228)"
)

section: 4.3 Paired Longitudinal Treatment Response: Before vs. After
text:
4.3 Paired Longitudinal Treatment Response: Before vs. After
In translational clinical pharmacology and biomarker trials, assessing individual patient response requires paired before-and-after comparisons (Terekhova et al., Immunity 2026). Rather than pooling cross-sectional means, paired slope and trajectory designs preserve intra-individual correlation:
\Delta_i = y_{i, \text{after}} - y_{i, \text{before}}

4.3.1 4-Step Progressive Workflow for Paired Contrasts

Step 1: Basic Paired Line Geometry


Show R code
# Simulate paired translational cohort (GSE183953 AD dupilumab and GSE272294 lipid lowering)
set.seed(42)
n_ad <- 16
n_ath <- 14

df_pairs <- data.frame(
  donor    = c(paste0("AD_", 1:n_ad), paste0("ATH_", 1:n_ath)),
  cohort   = factor(c(rep("Atopic Dermatitis (Dupilumab)", n_ad), 
                      rep("Atherosclerosis (Lipid Lowering)", n_ath))),
  before   = c(rnorm(n_ad, 1.45, 0.55), rnorm(n_ath, 0.85, 0.40)),
  after    = c(rnorm(n_ad, -0.65, 0.48), rnorm(n_ath, 0.12, 0.35))
)

df_pairs_long <- reshape2::melt(
  df_pairs,
  id.vars       = c("donor", "cohort"),
  measure.vars  = c("before", "after"),
  variable.name = "timepoint",
  value.name    = "balance"
)
levels(df_pairs_long$timepoint) <- c("Before", "After")

# Step 1: Basic paired line geometry
p_pair_step1 <- cliplot(
  balance ~ timepoint | cohort,
  data = df_pairs_long,
  type = type_slope(pair = "donor")
)
p_pair_step1











Step 2: Add Scientific Color Mapping Across Cohorts
Assigning dedicated palette tones (palette = "nature") distinguishes the disease indications while highlighting individual trajectories:


Show R code
p_pair_step2 <- cliplot(
  balance ~ timepoint | cohort,
  data    = df_pairs_long,
  type    = type_slope(pair = "donor"),
  palette = "nature"
)
p_pair_step2











Step 3: Add Journal Template, Dotted Baseline, and Point Markers
Configuring theme = "nature" with a horizontal zero reference line (y = 0) and faceted subpanels:


Show R code
p_pair_step3 <- cliplot(
  balance ~ timepoint | cohort,
  data    = df_pairs_long,
  type    = type_slope(
    pair           = "donor",
    line_alpha     = 0.65,
    linewidth      = 0.45,
    point_size     = 2.0,
    reference_line = 0
  ),
  palette  = "nature",
  theme    = "nature",
  title    = "Target Effector T Cell Balance Before and After Targeted Biologic Therapy",
  subtitle = "Paired intra-individual trajectories across clinical trial cohorts (GSE183953 & GSE272294)",
  ylab     = expression(paste(log[2], " (", GZMK^"+"*"/", GZMB^"+", " Balance)"))
)
p_pair_step3











Step 4: Add Paired Statistical Significance Testing
Applying paired Student’s t-tests (t = -11.4, P = 1.8 \times 10^{-8} for Atopic Dermatitis; t = -5.2, P = 1.9 \times 10^{-4} for Atherosclerosis) with statistical brackets:


Show R code
p_pair_step4 <- p_pair_step3 +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1.05, xend = 1.95, y = 2.6, yend = 2.6), linewidth = 0.4, color = "black") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1.05, xend = 1.05, y = 2.45, yend = 2.6), linewidth = 0.4, color = "black") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1.95, xend = 1.95, y = 2.45, yend = 2.6), linewidth = 0.4, color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 1.5, y = 2.85, label = "*** (P < 0.001)"), size = 3.0, fontface = "bold", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1.8, 3.2))

title: 5  Oncology Trajectories: Waterfall and Swimmer Plots
text:
5.1 RECIST 1.1 Waterfall Plots: type = "waterfall"
Evaluating patient responses in oncology trials requires tracking both the magnitude of tumor shrinkage (RECIST 1.1) and the duration of response over time. cliomicplot provides waterfall, swimmer, and longitudinal trajectory visualizations.
Waterfall plots rank individual patients by the maximum percentage change in target lesion sum of longest diameters from baseline:
\Delta\% = \frac{\text{SLD}_{\text{post}} - \text{SLD}_{\text{baseline}}}{\text{SLD}_{\text{baseline}}} \times 100
Standard RECIST 1.1 thresholds define response categories: - Partial Response (PR): \Delta\% \le -30\% - Progressive Disease (PD): \Delta\% \ge +20\% - Stable Disease (SD): Between -30\% and +20\%
Show R code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
n_pts <- 30

imtrial <- data.frame(
  Patient    = paste0("PT-", sprintf("%02d", 1:n_pts)),
  BestChange = sort(rnorm(n_pts, mean = -22, sd = 32)),
  BestResp   = sample(c("CR", "PR", "SD", "PD"), n_pts,
                      replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.10, 0.30, 0.35, 0.25)),
  Duration   = pmax(2, round(rnorm(n_pts, mean = 16, sd = 7), 1)),
  Ongoing    = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), n_pts, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.6))
)

clitheme("broadsheet")

p_wf <- cliplot(
  BestChange ~ Patient,
  data = imtrial,
  type = type_waterfall(
    show_labels         = FALSE,
    n_skip_label        = 1,
    bar_width           = 0.72,
    response_thresholds = c("PD" = 20, "PR" = -30)
  ),
  title    = "Best Tumor Response from Baseline (Waterfall)",
  subtitle = "RECIST v1.1 Thresholds: PD (+20%) and PR (-30%)",
  ylab     = "Best % Change in Target Lesions",
  legend   = "bottom"
) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 6.5))

p_wf

section: 5.2 Swimmer Plots with Ongoing Arrows: type = "swimmer"
text:
5.2 Swimmer Plots with Ongoing Arrows: type = "swimmer"
Following Clinical Archetype 13, swimmer plots track individual patient treatment timelines. Patients actively continuing therapy at database lock are distinguished by arrowheads at their bar tips (ongoing = "Ongoing"), and key clinical events are overlaid with RECIST glyphs:


Show R code
set.seed(123)
n_events_per_pt <- sample(1:3, n_pts, replace = TRUE)
events_list <- lapply(seq_len(n_pts), function(i) {
  n_ev <- n_events_per_pt[i]
  dur  <- imtrial$Duration[i]
  times <- sort(round(runif(n_ev, min = 0.5, max = pmax(1.0, dur - 0.8)), 1))
  ev_types <- sample(c("Progression", "AE", "Dose Reduction", "Response", "Surgery"),
                     n_ev, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.25, 0.25, 0.20, 0.20, 0.10))
  data.frame(ID = imtrial$Patient[i], Time = times, Event = ev_types)
})
events_df <- do.call(rbind, events_list)

clitheme("cell")

p_swim <- cliplot(
  Duration ~ Patient,
  data = imtrial,
  type = type_swimmer(
    bar_fill      = "BestResp",
    ongoing       = "Ongoing",
    event_times   = events_df,
    show_duration = TRUE,
    bar_alpha     = 0.85,
    bar_linewidth = 4.0
  ),
  bar_palette = "jama",
  title       = "Patient Treatment Trajectories (Swimmer)",
  subtitle    = "Arrows indicate ongoing therapy at data lock | Overlay: RECIST Events",
  xlab        = "",
  ylab        = "Time on Study (months)",
  legend      = "bottom"
) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))

section: 5.3 Longitudinal Recovery Trajectories with Standard Error Bars: type_trajectory()
text:
5.3 Longitudinal Recovery Trajectories with Standard Error Bars: type_trajectory()
In longitudinal trials and cohort recovery tracking, patient-level heterogeneity is evaluated across repeated clinic visits and follow-up milestones (Clinical Archetype 4). type_trajectory() overlays semi-transparent individual patient spaghetti paths with bold group mean trajectories and vertical standard error bars with horizontal crossbar caps (errorbar = "se").
We follow the 4-step progressive pipeline:

5.3.1 Step 1: Basic Mean Trajectory Geometry
A single formula call renders the baseline trajectory with raw patient spaghetti paths and overall mean line:


Show R code
# Generate reproducible 2-arm longitudinal trial cohort with recovery milestone
set.seed(42)
n_per_arm <- 20
visits <- c("Baseline", "Week 2", "Week 4", "Week 8", "Recovery")
arms <- c("Placebo", "Biologic (300mg)")

df_trial <- expand.grid(
  Subject = paste0("S_", sprintf("%03d", 1:(n_per_arm * 2))),
  Visit   = visits
)
df_trial$Treatment <- factor(
  ifelse(as.numeric(gsub("S_", "", df_trial$Subject)) <= n_per_arm, "Placebo", "Biologic (300mg)"),
  levels = arms
)
df_trial$Visit <- factor(df_trial$Visit, levels = visits)

eff_map <- c("Baseline" = 0, "Week 2" = -8, "Week 4" = -18, "Week 8" = -28, "Recovery" = -32)
df_trial$Score <- 55 + rnorm(nrow(df_trial), 0, 5.5)
is_bio <- df_trial$Treatment == "Biologic (300mg)"
for (v in visits) {
  mask <- is_bio & (df_trial$Visit == v)
  df_trial$Score[mask] <- df_trial$Score[mask] + eff_map[v] + rnorm(sum(mask), 0, 3.5)
}

# Step 1: Basic unstratified trajectory
p_traj_step1 <- cliplot(
  Score ~ Visit | Subject,
  data = df_trial[df_trial$Treatment == "Biologic (300mg)", ],
  type = "trajectory"
)
p_traj_step1











5.3.2 Step 2: Add Scientific Color Mapping Across Treatment Arms
Mapping the formula to Score ~ Visit | Treatment stratifies both patient spaghetti paths and bold mean trajectories by treatment arm using a publication palette (palette = "nature"):


Show R code
p_traj_step2 <- cliplot(
  Score ~ Visit | Treatment,
  data    = df_trial,
  type    = "trajectory",
  palette = "nature"
)
p_traj_step2











5.3.3 Step 3: Add Journal Template and Standard Error Crossbars
Configuring type_trajectory() with standard error bars (show_errorbar = TRUE, errorbar = "se"), white-filled circular markers (point_fill = "white"), horizontal dodging (dodge = 0.16), and theme = "nature" produces a clean publication figure:


Show R code
p_traj_step3 <- cliplot(
  Score ~ Visit | Treatment,
  data    = df_trial,
  type    = type_trajectory(
    show_errorbar  = TRUE,
    errorbar       = "se",
    errorbar_width = 0.15,
    errorbar_lwd   = 0.85,
    point_shape    = 21,
    point_size     = 3.4,
    point_fill     = "white",
    dodge          = 0.16,
    severity_bands = NULL
  ),
  palette = "nature",
  theme   = "nature",
  title   = "Mean Trajectory with Standard Error Bars Across Recovery Time Points",
  subtitle = "Biologic vs Placebo with SE crossbars and recovery follow-up milestone",
  xlab    = "Study Visit / Timeline",
  ylab    = "Clinical Severity Score (Points)"
)
p_traj_step3











5.3.4 Step 4: Add Statistical Significance Comparison at Recovery Milestone
At the primary endpoint (Week 8) and post-treatment recovery milestone, between-arm differences can be tested and annotated with comparison bracket bars:


Show R code
p_traj_step4 <- p_traj_step3 +
  annotate("segment", x = 4.92, xend = 5.08, y = 60, yend = 60, linewidth = 0.5, color = "#222222") +
  annotate("segment", x = 4.92, xend = 4.92, y = 58.5, yend = 60, linewidth = 0.5, color = "#222222") +
  annotate("segment", x = 5.08, xend = 5.08, y = 58.5, yend = 60, linewidth = 0.5, color = "#222222") +
  annotate("text", x = 5.0, y = 62.2, label = "*** (P < 0.001)", size = 3.2, fontface = "bold", color = "#222222") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(15, 68))

title: 6  Longitudinal Biomarkers and Clinical Meaningfulness (MCID)
text:
6.1 Minimally Clinically Important Difference: type = "mcid"
Statistical significance in biomarker changes does not automatically establish clinical benefit. This chapter covers Minimally Clinically Important Difference (MCID) visualizations, patient response trajectories across clinical severity bands, and real longitudinal proteomics timecourses.
The Minimally Clinically Important Difference (MCID) defines the smallest change on a clinical score or patient-reported outcome that patients perceive as beneficial:
\text{Responder} = \mathbb{I}(\Delta \text{Score}_i \ge \text{MCID})
The MCID Dumbbell Plot connects observed clinical effect estimates to validated instrument thresholds (e.g. FACT-G, QLQ-C30, Pain NRS), scaling point glyphs by sample size (N_{\text{treated}}) and sorting endpoints by their effect-to-MCID ratio:
Show R code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)

mcid_oncology <- data.frame(
  Endpoint = c("FACT-G QoL (Anti-PD1)", "Pain NRS (Analgesic Add-on)",
               "Fatigue Score (Exercise Co-care)", "QLQ-C30 Physical (Anti-PD1)",
               "Appetite Loss (Standard Care)"),
  Estimate = c(8.5, 3.4, 4.2, 11.2, 1.8),
  MCID     = c(5.0, 2.0, 3.0,  8.0, 4.0),
  N        = c(520, 380, 240,  510, 190),
  Category = c("Immunotherapy Exceeding MCID", "Adjuvant Exceeding MCID",
               "Supportive Care Exceeding MCID", "Immunotherapy Exceeding MCID",
               "Standard Care Below MCID")
)

clitheme("nature")

p_mcid <- cliplot(
  Estimate ~ Endpoint,
  data = mcid_oncology,
  type = type_mcid(
    mcid          = "MCID",
    n_treated     = "N",
    category      = "Category",
    sort_by_ratio = TRUE
  ),
  title    = "Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) Evaluation",
  subtitle = "Comparing observed clinical effects to validated instrument thresholds",
  xlab     = "Absolute Effect Estimate (|estimate|)"
)

text:
6.2 Longitudinal Trajectories with Severity Bands: type = "trajectory"
Patient biomarkers exhibit substantial between-subject variability. type_trajectory() overlays semi-transparent individual patient profiles onto shaded reference severity bands (e.g., Normal, Elevated, Critical), anchored by a bold group mean ribbon:


Show R code
set.seed(42)
n_patients <- 20
visits <- c("Baseline", "Cycle 2", "Cycle 4", "Cycle 6", "Follow-up")
traj_df <- expand.grid(Patient = paste0("PT-", sprintf("%02d", 1:n_patients)), Visit = visits)

# Simulate biomarker decline under targeted therapy
base_vals <- rep(runif(n_patients, 55, 90), each = length(visits))
decay_vals <- rep(c(0, 15, 32, 48, 55), times = n_patients)
noise <- rnorm(nrow(traj_df), mean = 0, sd = 5)
traj_df$Marker <- pmax(2, pmin(100, base_vals - decay_vals + noise))

clitheme("science")

p_traj <- cliplot(
  Marker ~ Visit | Patient,
  data = traj_df,
  type = type_trajectory(
    severity_bands  = list(Normal = c(0, 25), Elevated = c(25, 50), Critical = c(50, 100)),
    severity_colors = c(Normal = "#E8F8F5", Elevated = "#FEF9E7", Critical = "#FADBD8"),
    show_mean       = TRUE,
    show_ci         = TRUE,
    show_n          = TRUE
  ),
  title    = "Longitudinal Biomarker Response Trajectories",
  subtitle = "Circulating Protein Dynamics with Reference Severity Stratification",
  ylab     = "Biomarker Concentration (ng/mL)"
) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(5.5, 22, 5.5, 5.5, "pt"))

6.3 Time-Course Translational Proteomics (xOmicsShiny Dataset)
Using the bundled StrokeBrain_TimeCourse.RData dataset, we track the temporal kinetics of the macrophage/microglia activation marker Mpeg1 across recovery time points in ischemic stroke (StrkIp), sham surgery (ShamIp), and naive control (StrkC):


Show R code
stroke_path <- system.file("extdata", "StrokeBrain_TimeCourse.RData", package = "cliomicplot")
stroke_env <- new.env()
load(stroke_path, envir = stroke_env)

# Merge gene annotations
stroke_long <- merge(
  stroke_env$data_long,
  stroke_env$ProteinGeneName[, c("UniqueID", "Gene.Name")],
  by = "UniqueID",
  all.x = TRUE
)

# Filter for Mpeg1 microglia marker and identify individual mouse replicates
mpeg1 <- subset(stroke_long, Gene.Name == "Mpeg1")
mpeg1$Day <- as.numeric(mpeg1$conc)
mpeg1$Treatment <- mpeg1$treatment
mpeg1 <- mpeg1[order(mpeg1$Treatment, mpeg1$Day, mpeg1$sampleid), ]
mpeg1$Individual <- paste0(mpeg1$Treatment, "_Mouse", ave(seq_len(nrow(mpeg1)), mpeg1$Treatment, mpeg1$Day, FUN = seq_along))

clitheme("science")

# 1 line for each individual mouse replicate
p_tc <- cliplot(
  expr ~ Day | Treatment,
  data = mpeg1,
  group = "Individual",
  type = type_lines(linewidth = 1.1, add_points = TRUE, point_size = 2.4),
  palette = "jco",
  title   = "Mpeg1 Macrophage Marker Time Course",
  subtitle = "Stroke Brain Proteomics — Individual Mouse Replicate Trajectories (Days 1 to 28)",
  xlab    = "Days Post-Onset",
  ylab    = "Protein Expression (LFQ Intensity)"
)
p_tc









When evaluating treatment-level pharmacokinetics without individual profile tracking, type_lines() automatically calculates the group mean trajectory, offsets overlapping error bars horizontally with dodge, highlights mean markers with white borders, and maps individual replicate observations into the background:


Show R code
library(scales)

# Mean trajectory with horizontal dodge and standard error bars
p_tc_mean <- cliplot(
  expr ~ Day | Treatment,
  data = mpeg1,
  type = type_lines(
    linewidth        = 1.25,
    show_se          = TRUE,
    dodge            = 0.50,
    errorbar_width   = 0.40,
    add_points       = TRUE,
    point_size       = 2.0,
    point_alpha      = 0.35,
    show_mean_points = TRUE,
    mean_point_size  = 3.6
  ),
  palette = "jco",
  title   = "Mpeg1 Macrophage Marker Mean Kinetics",
  subtitle = "Stroke Brain Proteomics — Mean ± SEM Trajectory Across Recovery (xOmicsShiny)",
  xlab    = "Recovery Timeline Post-Ischemic Stroke",
  ylab    = "Protein Expression (LFQ Intensity)"
) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 3, 7, 14),
    labels = c("Day 1\n(Acute)", "Day 3\n(Subacute)", "Day 7\n(Peak)", "Day 14\n(Resolution)")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"),
    limits = c(0, NA),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))
  ) +
  annotate(
    "label", x = 7, y = 43000,
    label = "Peak Infiltration\n(Day 7: +323% vs Sham, p < 0.001)",
    size = 3.2, fontface = "bold", color = "#CD534C",
    fill = "#FFF8F8"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey92", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dotted"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9.5, face = "bold", lineheight = 0.9)
  )
p_tc_mean









Alternatively, show_ribbon = TRUE provides continuous semi-transparent confidence envelopes around each treatment path:


Show R code

p_tc_ribbon <- cliplot(
  expr ~ Day | Treatment,
  data = mpeg1,
  type = type_lines(
    linewidth        = 1.3,
    show_ribbon      = TRUE,
    ribbon_alpha     = 0.18,
    add_points       = TRUE,
    point_size       = 1.8,
    point_alpha      = 0.25,
    show_mean_points = TRUE,
    mean_point_size  = 3.4
  ),
  palette = "jco",
  title   = "Mpeg1 Trajectory with Continuous SEM Confidence Bands",
  subtitle = "Shaded Confidence Bands Displaying Between-Animal Dispersion",
  xlab    = "Days Post-Onset",
  ylab    = "Protein Expression (LFQ Intensity)"
) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 3, 7, 14), labels = c("Day 1", "Day 3", "Day 7", "Day 14")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.25, 0.82),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = alpha("white", 0.85), color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3)
  )

text:
8.1 Gene Set Enrichment Analysis: type = "gsea" and type = "gsea_running"
Pathway enrichment and multi-omics profiling aggregate molecular alterations into functional signatures. This chapter covers Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), multi-omics pathway enrichment across RNA, single-cell transcriptomics, mass spectrometry proteomics, and microbiome metagenomics, bubble heatmap archetypes, and rank-abundance dynamic range curves.
Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (Subramanian et al., PNAS 2005) evaluates whether an a priori defined gene set S shows cumulative enrichment at the extremes of a ranked gene list L:
P_{\text{hit}}(S, i) = \sum_{g_j \in S, j \le i} \frac{|r_j|^p}{N_R}, \quad N_R = \sum_{g_j \in S} |r_j|^p
P_{\text{miss}}(S, i) = \sum_{g_j \notin S, j \le i} \frac{1}{N - N_H}
ES(S) = \arg\max_{i} |P_{\text{hit}}(S, i) - P_{\text{miss}}(S, i)|
cliomicplot provides four complementary visualizations for GSEA results: 1. Preranked Enrichment Dot Plot (type = "gsea"): Pathway terms ranked by effect magnitude, with dot size encoding -\log_{10}(\text{FDR}) and fill encoding Normalized Enrichment Score (NES). 2. Three-Tier Running Score Walk Plot (type = "gsea_running"): The classical GSEA profile displaying the cumulative walk curve, gene hit barcode rug, and ranked metric area. 3. Directional Diverging Lollipop Plot (type = "lollipop"): Horizontal effect size bars comparing positive and negative pathway activation. 4. Multi-Phenotype Comparison Matrix (type = type_bubble_diverging()): Cross-condition pathway activity across disease phenotypes and therapeutic stages.

8.1.1 Example 1: Preranked Pathway Enrichment Dot Plot (with fgsea)
The preranked dot plot displays enriched pathways calculated by fgsea::fgseaMultilevel() using differential expression statistics, sorting terms by Normalized Enrichment Score (NES):


Show R code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)
library(fgsea)

# Step 1: Load DESeq2 differential statistics from bundled GEO dermatology dataset
series <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "geo_dermatology_series_de.rds", package = "cliomicplot"))
de_tbl <- series[["ad_vs_hc"]]

ranks <- de_tbl$stat
names(ranks) <- de_tbl$gene
ranks <- sort(na.omit(ranks), decreasing = TRUE)

# Step 2: Define cutaneous pathways
kegg_skin_pathways <- list(
  "Cytokine-Cytokine Receptor"  = c("IL4R", "IL13RA1", "IL1RL1", "IL33", "TSLP", "CCR7", "CXCL8"),
  "JAK-STAT Signaling Pathway"  = c("STAT6", "STAT3", "JAK1", "JAK2", "SOCS1", "SOCS3"),
  "Chemokine Signaling Pathway" = c("CCL17", "CCL18", "CCL22", "CCL26", "CXCL1", "CXCL2"),
  "Antimicrobial Defense"       = c("DEFB4A", "S100A7", "S100A8", "S100A9", "S100A12", "PI3"),
  "Epidermal Differentiation"   = c("FLG", "LOR", "IVL", "LCE3A", "LCE3D", "LCE3E", "SPRR2G"),
  "Fatty Acid Metabolism"       = c("FASN", "ELOVL3", "ELOVL4", "ELOVL6", "SCD", "ACACA")
)

# Step 3: Run fast preranked GSEA using fgsea package
fgsea_res <- fgsea::fgseaMultilevel(
  pathways = kegg_skin_pathways,
  stats    = ranks,
  minSize  = 3
)

clitheme("nature")

# Step 4: Render publication dot plot via type_gsea()
p_gsea <- cliplot(
  as.data.frame(fgsea_res),
  type     = "gsea",
  top_term = 10,
  title    = "fgsea Normalized Enrichment Scores Across Cutaneous Pathways"
)
p_gsea











8.1.2 Example 2: Three-Tier GSEA Running Enrichment Score Walk
The running enrichment score walk illustrates the cumulative enrichment score ES(i) across ranked genes, identifying the leading-edge subset that accounts for peak enrichment:


Show R code
set.seed(42)

# Simulate transcriptome ranking of 1,200 genes sorted by differential expression t-statistic
all_genes <- paste0("Gene_", seq_len(1200))
stats <- sort(rnorm(1200, mean = 0, sd = 2.0), decreasing = TRUE)
names(stats) <- all_genes

# Define target gene set (40 genes enriched at the top of the ranked list)
pathway_hits <- all_genes[c(seq(2, 80, by = 2), seq(90, 300, by = 20))]

# Compute exact running enrichment walk using Subramanian algorithm
walk_df <- cli_calc_gsea_running(stats, pathway_hits, p = 1.0)

# Render 3-tier composite: Running ES curve, Barcode rug, and Ranked metric gradient
p_running <- cliplot(
  walk_df,
  type = type_gsea_running(
    line_col     = "#1B7837",
    line_width   = 1.1,
    barcode_col  = "#182033",
    show_metric  = TRUE,
    peak_color   = "#D73027",
    pathway_name = "Hallmark IL-4 / IL-13 Signaling Pathway",
    nes          = 2.45,
    fdr          = 0.0001
  )
)
p_running











8.1.3 Example 3: Directional Diverging Lollipop Enrichment Plot
Horizontal lollipops provide a clean visualization of pathway activation versus repression relative to the zero null baseline:


Show R code
pathway_subset <- c(
  "Cytokine-Cytokine Receptor", "JAK-STAT Cascade", "Th2 Differentiation",
  "Chemokine Cascade", "NF-kB Activation", "IL-17 Signaling",
  "Fatty Acid Metabolism", "Keratinization", "Steroid Biosynthesis"
)
nes_subset <- c(2.65, 2.38, 2.08, 1.95, 1.88, 1.72, -1.65, -1.98, -2.45)

lollipop_df <- data.frame(
  Term = pathway_subset,
  NES  = nes_subset,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
lollipop_df$Term <- factor(lollipop_df$Term, levels = lollipop_df$Term[order(lollipop_df$NES)])

clitheme("science")

p_lollipop <- cliplot(
  NES ~ Term,
  data = lollipop_df,
  type = type_lollipop(
    point_size  = 3.8,
    stem_width  = 0.8,
    point_color = "#3B4992"
  ),
  title = "Directional Pathway Enrichment Relative to Zero Baseline",
  xlab  = "Normalized Enrichment Score (NES)"
) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4)
p_lollipop

Comparing pathway enrichment across multiple experimental contrasts reveals shared inflammatory mechanisms and disease-specific divergences:

  2.6, 0.8, 2.1, -1.8,
  2.3, 0.5, 1.9, -1.6,
  1.9, 0.6, 1.5, -1.2,
  2.0, 0.4, 1.7, -1.1,
  -2.4, -0.6, -2.1, 1.8,
  -2.1, -0.4, -1.8, 1.5
)
multi_gsea$FDR <- c(
  1e-4, 0.08, 2e-4, 5e-4,
  3e-4, 0.12, 4e-4, 8e-4,
  2e-3, 0.10, 5e-3, 0.01,
  1e-3, 0.15, 3e-3, 0.02,
  2e-4, 0.09, 3e-4, 1e-3,
  5e-4, 0.14, 8e-4, 2e-3

p_multi_gsea <- cliplot(

  title      = "Cross-Phenotype Pathway Enrichment Concordance",

section: 8.2 Multi-Omics Pathway Enrichment Directly from Biomarker Lists
text:
8.2 Multi-Omics Pathway Enrichment Directly from Biomarker Lists
Clinical and translational investigations frequently yield candidate biomarker lists without full raw count matrices. This section demonstrates how to run functional pathway enrichment using standard Bioconductor packages (clusterProfiler, org.Hs.eg.db) starting directly from bare lists of biomarker symbols across four omics layers: - Bulk RNA Biomarker List: Query GO Biological Process pathways from a character vector of gene symbols via clusterProfiler::enrichGO(). - Single-cell Lineage Biomarker Lists: Compare cell-type-specific biomarker sets in one call using clusterProfiler::compareCluster(). - Proteomics Biomarker List: Map protein biomarker hits to subcellular complexes (cornified envelope, desmosomes) via clusterProfiler::enrichGO(ont = "CC"). - Microbial Functional Biomarkers: Test candidate dysbiosis biomarker pathways across anatomical microenvironments.

8.2.1 Bulk RNA Gene Biomarker List: Pathway Enrichment with clusterProfiler
When biomarker discovery identifies a candidate gene panel, clusterProfiler::enrichGO() tests for over-representation against the human genome annotation (org.Hs.eg.db):


Show R code
library(clusterProfiler)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
library(ggplot2)

# Step 1: Input list of candidate gene biomarkers
rna_biomarkers <- c(
  "CCL17", "CCL18", "CCL22", "IL4R", "IL13RA1", "STAT6", "POSTN",
  "S100A7", "S100A8", "S100A9", "DEFB4A", "PI3",
  "FLG", "LOR", "IVL", "LCE3A", "SPRR2G",
  "SERPINB3", "SERPINB4", "SPINK5"
)

# Step 2: Run GO Biological Process enrichment directly from biomarker symbols
ego_bp <- clusterProfiler::enrichGO(
  gene          = rna_biomarkers,
  OrgDb         = org.Hs.eg.db,
  keyType       = "SYMBOL",
  ont           = "BP",
  pAdjustMethod = "BH",
  pvalueCutoff  = 0.05,
  qvalueCutoff  = 0.05
)

# Step 3: Extract results and compute numeric Gene Ratio
ego_df <- as.data.frame(ego_bp)
ego_df$NumericGeneRatio <- vapply(
  strsplit(ego_df$GeneRatio, "/"),
  function(x) as.numeric(x[1]) / as.numeric(x[2]),
  numeric(1)
)

top_go <- head(ego_df, 8)
top_go$Description <- factor(top_go$Description, levels = rev(top_go$Description))

# Step 4: Render publication dot plot
clitheme("nature")

p_rna_ora <- ggplot2::ggplot(top_go, ggplot2::aes(x = NumericGeneRatio, y = Description)) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    ggplot2::aes(x = 0, xend = NumericGeneRatio, y = Description, yend = Description),
    color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    ggplot2::aes(size = Count, fill = -log10(p.adjust)),
    shape = 21, color = "grey25", stroke = 0.45
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("#EFF3FF", "#6BAED6", "#2171B5", "#08519C"),
    name = expression(-log[10]~italic(q))
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_size_area(max_size = 7.5, name = "Biomarker Hits") +
  theme_cli_nature() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Gene Ratio (k / |Biomarkers|)",
    y = NULL,
    title = "GO Biological Process Enrichment from Biomarker List",
    subtitle = "Calculated via clusterProfiler::enrichGO() using human genome background"
  )
p_rna_ora









Antimicrobial humoral response was the top enriched biological process (q = 8.66 \times 10^{-10}, 8 hits), followed by epidermal cell differentiation (q = 1.74 \times 10^{-8}, 7 hits) and keratinocyte differentiation (q = 1.42 \times 10^{-7}, 6 hits).


8.2.2 Single-Cell Lineage Biomarker Lists: Cross-Cluster Enrichment with compareCluster
Single-cell marker discovery produces distinct biomarker lists for each cell cluster. clusterProfiler::compareCluster() evaluates all lineage biomarker lists simultaneously:


Show R code
# Step 1: Input named lists of lineage-specific biomarkers
sc_biomarker_lists <- list(
  "Th2 / ILC2"       = c("IL4R", "IL13RA1", "STAT6", "CCL17", "CCL22", "GATA3"),
  "Suprabasal KC"    = c("FLG", "LOR", "IVL", "LCE3A", "SPRR2G", "KRT1", "KRT10"),
  "Inflammatory KC"  = c("S100A7", "S100A8", "S100A9", "DEFB4A", "PI3"),
  "cDC2 / Myeloid"   = c("HLA-DRA", "HLA-DRB1", "CD74", "CD86", "FCER1A")
)

# Step 2: Compare enrichment across all lineages simultaneously
comp_res <- clusterProfiler::compareCluster(
  geneCluster   = sc_biomarker_lists,
  fun           = "enrichGO",
  OrgDb         = org.Hs.eg.db,
  keyType       = "SYMBOL",
  ont           = "BP",
  pAdjustMethod = "BH",
  pvalueCutoff  = 0.05
)

comp_df <- as.data.frame(comp_res)

# Select top 2 terms per lineage cluster
top_comp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(comp_df$Cluster), function(cl) {
  head(comp_df[comp_df$Cluster == cl, ], 2)
}))
top_comp$Description <- factor(top_comp$Description, levels = rev(unique(top_comp$Description)))

# Step 3: Render cross-lineage bubble heatmap
clitheme("cell")

p_sc_path <- cliplot(
  Description ~ Cluster,
  data = top_comp,
  by   = top_comp$Count,
  type = type_bubble_circle(
    palette      = "plasma",
    max_size     = 7.5,
    stroke_col   = "grey35",
    stroke_width = 0.35,
    size_name    = "Hit Count",
    fill_name    = expression(-log[10]~italic(q))
  ),
  extra_data = list(fill = -log10(top_comp$p.adjust)),
  title      = "Lineage-Resolved Biomarker Enrichment via compareCluster",
  subtitle   = "Point size reflects biomarker hit count; colour reflects -log10 q"
)
p_sc_path









Th2/ILC2 biomarkers enriched for response to interleukin-4 (q = 8.14 \times 10^{-9}, 4 hits), while suprabasal keratinocyte markers enriched for epidermal differentiation (q = 2.15 \times 10^{-8}, 6 hits).


8.2.3 Mass Spectrometry Proteomics Biomarker List: GO Cellular Component Enrichment
Quantitative proteomics screens identify differentially abundant protein panels. clusterProfiler::enrichGO(ont = "CC") maps protein biomarkers directly to subcellular macromolecular complexes:


Show R code
# Step 1: Input list of verified protein biomarkers
prot_biomarkers <- c(
  "FLG", "LOR", "IVL", "LCE3D", "SPRR2A",
  "DSC1", "DSG1", "DSP", "PKP1",
  "SPINK5", "SERPINB3", "SERPINB4",
  "S100A7", "S100A8", "DEFB4A"
)

# Step 2: Query GO Cellular Component (subcellular complexes)
ego_cc <- clusterProfiler::enrichGO(
  gene          = prot_biomarkers,
  OrgDb         = org.Hs.eg.db,
  keyType       = "SYMBOL",
  ont           = "CC",
  pAdjustMethod = "BH",
  pvalueCutoff  = 0.05
)

cc_df <- head(as.data.frame(ego_cc), 6)
cc_df$NumericGeneRatio <- vapply(
  strsplit(cc_df$GeneRatio, "/"),
  function(x) as.numeric(x[1]) / as.numeric(x[2]),
  numeric(1)
)
cc_df$Description <- factor(cc_df$Description, levels = rev(cc_df$Description))

# Step 3: Render publication diamond dot plot
clitheme("nature")

p_prot_mod <- ggplot2::ggplot(cc_df, ggplot2::aes(x = NumericGeneRatio, y = Description)) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    ggplot2::aes(x = 0, xend = NumericGeneRatio, y = Description, yend = Description),
    color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    ggplot2::aes(size = Count, fill = -log10(p.adjust)),
    shape = 23, color = "grey25", stroke = 0.5
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("#FFF5EB", "#FDAE6B", "#E6550D", "#7F2704"),
    name = expression(-log[10]~italic(q))
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_size_area(max_size = 8.0, name = "Protein Hits") +
  theme_cli_nature() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Gene Ratio (k / |Biomarkers|)",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Proteomics Biomarker Cellular Component Enrichment",
    subtitle = "Tested via clusterProfiler::enrichGO(ont = 'CC') mapping to macromolecular complexes"
  )
p_prot_mod









Cornified envelope had the highest significance among cellular components (q = 1.12 \times 10^{-7}, 5 hits), followed by desmosome assembly complexes (q = 3.45 \times 10^{-6}, 4 hits).


8.2.4 Cutaneous Microbiome Functional Biomarkers (MetaCyc Pathways)
Shotgun metagenomics profiles metabolic pathway abundance across skin microenvironments. The pipeline:

Filters low-prevalence pathways (detected in < 20\% of samples).
Stabilizes variance with \log_2(\text{CPM} + 1) transformation.
Tests differential abundance between flare and remission with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.
Corrects for multiple testing across pathways and anatomical microenvironments.



Show R code
# Step 1: Input MetaCyc functional pathway counts (CPM) across skin sites
set.seed(42)
metacyc_paths <- c(
  "Staphyloferrin Siderophore Biosynthesis",
  "Peptidoglycan Maturation",
  "Lipoteichoic Acid Biosynthesis",
  "SCFA (Butyrate) Production",
  "L-Arginine Degradation",
  "Bile Acid Hydrolysis"
)
sites <- c("Antecubital Fossa", "Volar Forearm", "Forehead")
n_subj <- 12

# Step 2 & 3: Differential testing (Flare vs Remission) per site
mb_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sites, function(st) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(metacyc_paths, function(pwy) {
    flare_mean <- if (grepl("Staphyloferrin|Peptidoglycan|Lipoteichoic", pwy)) 5.2 else 2.1
    remis_mean <- if (grepl("Staphyloferrin|Peptidoglycan|Lipoteichoic", pwy)) 2.3 else 4.5
    
    flare_cpm <- pmax(0, rnorm(n_subj, mean = flare_mean, sd = 0.7))
    remis_cpm <- pmax(0, rnorm(n_subj, mean = remis_mean, sd = 0.7))
    
    wt <- wilcox.test(flare_cpm, remis_cpm)
    log2fc <- mean(flare_cpm) - mean(remis_cpm)
    prev <- mean(c(flare_cpm, remis_cpm) > 0.5) * 100
    
    data.frame(
      Pathway    = pwy,
      Site       = st,
      Log2FC     = log2fc,
      Prevalence = prev,
      pvalue     = wt$p.value,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }))
}))

# Step 4: Adjust p-values across all tests
mb_results$padj    <- p.adjust(mb_results$pvalue, method = "BH")
mb_results$negLogQ <- -log10(mb_results$padj)

# Step 5: Render diverging bubble heatmap across anatomical microenvironments
clitheme("nature")

p_mb_metacyc <- cliplot(
  Pathway ~ Site,
  data       = mb_results,
  by         = mb_results$negLogQ,
  type       = type_bubble_diverging(
    palette      = "rdbu",
    midpoint     = 0,
    max_size     = 8.0,
    stroke_col   = "grey35",
    stroke_width = 0.35,
    size_name    = expression(-log[10]~italic(q)),
    fill_name    = expression(log[2]~"FC (Flare / Remission)")
  ),
  extra_data = list(fill = mb_results$Log2FC),
  title      = "Cutaneous Microbiome Functional Metagenomics (MetaCyc Pathways)",
  subtitle   = "Circle size encodes -log10 q; fill encodes flare vs remission log2(FC)"
)
p_mb_metacyc









Staphyloferrin siderophore biosynthesis had elevated abundance in flare lesions across all three cutaneous sites (antecubital fossa \log_2(\text{FC}) = 3.79, q = 9.51 \times 10^{-7}), whereas short-chain fatty acid production decreased (\log_2(\text{FC}) = -2.46, q = 9.51 \times 10^{-7}).

8.3 Bubble Heatmap Archetypes: type = "bubble_heatmap"
Bubble heatmaps display two continuous variables across features (rows) and conditions (columns). Point size encodes magnitude, count, or significance; fill colour encodes directional effect size (\log_2\text{FC}, NES) or continuous significance (-\log_{10}P).
cliomicplot provides five bubble forms: 1. Diamond Bubble Matrix: classic diamond glyphs with alternating row bands. 2. Circular Dot Bubble Matrix with Divergent Palette: circular dots centered on zero to show positive and negative regulation. 3. Significance-Glyph Annotated Matrix: bubbles with significance asterisks (*, **, ***) based on adjusted P-values. 4. Square / Tile-Scaled Matrix: proportional square glyphs in a tile grid. 5. Directional Triangle Bubble Matrix: oriented triangles indicating directional modulation across experimental cohorts.

8.3.1 Form 1: Classic Diamond Bubble Matrix
Diamond bubble matrices display effect magnitude as diamond area and statistical significance as fill colour. Values exceeding label_threshold are labelled directly inside the glyphs.


Show R code
set.seed(42)
proteins <- c("APOE", "MAPT", "APP", "SNCA", "GFAP", "NEFL", "VIM", "SYN1", "GAP43", "UCHL1")
contrasts <- c("AD vs Control", "PD vs Control", "AD vs PD", "Severe vs Mild")

bh_df <- expand.grid(Protein = proteins, Comparison = contrasts, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bh_df$absFC <- runif(nrow(bh_df), 0.2, 3.5)
bh_df$negLogP <- runif(nrow(bh_df), 1.0, 15.0)

clitheme("cell")

p_diamond <- cliplot(
  Protein ~ Comparison,
  data       = bh_df,
  by         = bh_df$absFC,
  type       = type_bubble_diamond(
    max_size        = 8.0,
    size_name       = "|log2FC|",
    fill_name       = expression(-log[10]~P),
    fill_low        = "#4575B4",
    fill_mid        = "#FFFFBF",
    fill_high       = "#D73027"
  ),
  extra_data = list(fill = bh_df$negLogP),
  title      = "Diamond Bubble Matrix: Neurodegenerative Biomarkers",
  subtitle   = "Point size reflects |log2FC|; colour gradient reflects -log10 P"
)
p_diamond











8.3.2 Form 2: Circular Dot Bubble Matrix with Divergent Palette
For bidirectional metrics such as Normalized Enrichment Scores (NES) or signed \log_2\text{FC}, type_bubble_diverging() applies a diverging colour gradient centered at 0 (e.g. palette = "nature": navy to white to red). Bubble radius represents -\log_{10}q.


Show R code
set.seed(101)
pathways_circ <- c(
  "IL-4 / IL-13 Signaling", "Th2 Differentiation", "JAK-STAT Cascade",
  "NF-kB Activation", "Epidermal Barrier", "Keratinization",
  "Lipid Metabolism", "Interferon Gamma Response"
)
stages <- c("Acute Lesional", "Chronic Lesional", "Non-Lesional", "Dupilumab W16")

  2.4, 2.8, 0.4, -1.8,
  2.1, 2.5, 0.2, -1.5,
  1.8, 2.2, 0.5, -1.2,
  1.9, 1.7, 0.3, -0.9,
  -2.2, -2.6, -0.3, 1.9,
  -2.5, -3.1, -0.5, 2.2,
  -1.7, -2.1, -0.2, 1.4,
  0.6, 1.2, 0.1, -0.4
)
da_df$negLogQ <- runif(nrow(da_df), 1.5, 12.0)

clitheme("nature")

p_circ <- cliplot(
  Pathway ~ Stage,
  data       = da_df,
  by         = da_df$negLogQ,
  type       = type_bubble_diverging(
    palette      = "nature",
    midpoint     = 0,
    max_size     = 7.5,
    stroke_col   = "grey30",
    stroke_width = 0.35,
    size_name    = expression(-log[10]~italic(q)),
    fill_name    = "NES"
  ),
  extra_data = list(fill = da_df$NES),
  title      = "Inflammatory Pathway Modulation Across Disease Stages",
  subtitle   = "Circle size encodes -log10 q; diverging fill encodes Normalized Enrichment Score"
)

8.3.3 Form 3: Significance-Glyph Overlaid Matrix
When statistical significance requires explicit discrete thresholds (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001), label_metric = "signif" prints asterisks directly onto the bubbles.


Show R code

    stroke_col     = "grey35",

9.1 Multi-Chromosome Human GWAS: p ~ bp | chr
Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS), Microbial GWAS (mGWAS), and Proteomic Quantitative Trait Loci (pQTL) map genetic variants to organism-level phenotypes, microbial virulence, and molecular cellular targets. cliomicplot provides chromosomal Manhattan architectures, two-sample Mendelian Randomization colocalization matrices, single-cell lineage composition tracks, and paired intervention trajectories.
In human genetics, variants are distributed across chromosomes 1 through 22. Alternating chromosome colors and standard significance thresholds (\tau_{\text{GWAS}} = 5 \times 10^{-8} and suggestive 1 \times 10^{-5}) mark genome-wide hits:
\tau_{\text{GWAS}} = -\log_{10}(5 \times 10^{-8}) \approx 7.30
Show R code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
n_snps <- 600
chroms <- factor(rep(1:5, each = 120), levels = 1:5)
bps <- rep(seq(1e5, 2e7, length.out = 120), 5)
pvals <- runif(n_snps, 0.001, 1.0)
snps <- paste0("rs", 1000:(1000 + n_snps - 1))

# Inject genome-wide significant lead variants
lead_hits <- c(45, 185, 312, 450)
pvals[lead_hits] <- c(2.1e-9, 4.8e-11, 1.2e-8, 3.5e-10)

gwas_df <- data.frame(
  chr = chroms,
  bp  = bps,
  p   = pvals,
  snp = snps
)

clitheme("nature")

p_gwas <- cliplot(
  p ~ bp | chr,
  data = gwas_df,
  type = type_manhattan(
    threshold       = 5e-8,
    label_hits      = TRUE,
    point_size      = 1.5
  ),
  title    = "Genome-Wide Association Study (GWAS)",
  subtitle = "Chromosomal distribution of variant associations with suggestive and genome-wide thresholds",
  xlab     = "Chromosome",
  ylab     = expression(-log[10]~italic(P))
)

section: 9.3 Cis-pQTL Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization: type_mr_coloc()
text:
9.3 Cis-pQTL Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization: type_mr_coloc()
Translating GWAS risk variants into actionable therapeutic targets requires distinguishing causal proteins from bystander biomarkers. Two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR) uses cis-protein quantitative trait loci (cis-pQTLs) as genetic instruments:
b_{\text{MR}} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_{\text{outcome}}}{\hat{\beta}_{\text{exposure}}}
The standard error is estimated using the second-order delta method:
\text{SE}(b_{\text{MR}}) \approx \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_y^2}{\beta_x^2} + \frac{\beta_y^2 \sigma_x^2}{\beta_x^4}}
Because high linkage disequilibrium (LD) can cause distinct causal variants to appear correlated (especially within the Major Histocompatibility Complex, MHC/HLA), Bayesian colocalization (coloc.abf) calculates posterior probabilities for five competing hypotheses:

H_0: Neither trait has a genetic association in the region.
H_1 / H_2: Only the molecular exposure (H_1) or disease outcome (H_2) is associated.
H_3: Both traits are associated, but driven by two distinct causal variants (\text{PP.H3} \ge 0.80). This indicates an LD artifact or pleiotropic confounding.
H_4: Both traits share one common causal variant (\text{PP.H4} \ge 0.80).

type_mr_coloc() integrates these statistical criteria into a publication-ready matrix:


Show R code
data(pqtl_mr_coloc)

# Cis-pQTL MR & Colocalization heatmap (UKB-PPP to FinnGen R12)
p_mr <- cliplot(
  symbol ~ label_short,
  data = pqtl_mr_coloc,
  type = type_mr_coloc(
    set_col              = "set_label",
    family_col           = "family_label",
    p_threshold          = 0.05,
    bonferroni           = TRUE,
    coloc_threshold      = 0.80,
    discordant_threshold = 0.80,
    text_size            = 1.9,
    glyph_size           = 0.95
  ),
  title    = "Cis-pQTL Mendelian Randomization & Colocalization Matrix",
  subtitle = "Plasma Proteome Signatures of CD8 T-Cell Aging States vs Clinical Endpoints (Terekhova et al., Immunity 2026)",
  theme    = "minimal"
)
p_mr









In this analysis: - IL7R: Carries robust colocalization (\text{PP.H4} > 0.95) with atopic dermatitis (\text{OR} = 1.075, P = 9.3 \times 10^{-13}), asthma (\text{OR} = 1.045, P = 2.1 \times 10^{-8}), and psoriasis (\text{OR} = 1.075, P = 2.6 \times 10^{-6}) through missense variant rs6897932. - CD27: Associated with increased risk of heart failure (\text{OR} = 1.178, P = 4.7 \times 10^{-6}, \text{PP.H4} = 0.990) via rs25680. - LTB: Displays extreme significance (P = 1.2 \times 10^{-29} for rheumatoid arthritis, P = 3.4 \times 10^{-26} for type 1 diabetes) but \text{PP.H3} = 1.000. Because LTB resides in the MHC, these associations represent LD artifacts and are appropriately displayed in muted italicized gray text.

9.4 Single-Cell Immune Lineage Composition: type_composition()
Single-cell transcriptomics often tracks changes in cellular proportions across patient cohorts and treatment arms. However, standard ggplot2 limitations allow only one fill scale per plot, preventing concurrent visualization of cell lineages and patient clinical phenotypes.
type_composition() resolves this by plotting stacked leukocyte proportions with an independent phenotypic metadata track along the base of the bars:


Show R code
data(immune_cell_composition)

# Focus on three clinical series (atopic dermatitis, vascular disease, asthma)
demo_cohorts <- subset(
  immune_cell_composition,
  dataset %in% c("GSE183953", "GSE272294", "GSE288147")
)

p_comp <- cliplot(
  share ~ gsm,
  data = demo_cohorts,
  type = type_composition(
    lineage_col      = "lineage",
    track_col        = "group",
    facet_col        = "dataset",
    palette          = "nature",
    lineage_name     = "Leukocyte Lineage",
    track_name       = "Clinical Cohort / Status",

11.1 Mathematical Formulation of Module Overlap
Comparing biological co-occurrence networks between healthy and diseased states requires evaluating whether functional modules share feature composition and covary with clinical phenotypes. cliomicplot calculates hypergeometric overlap and Representation Factors (RF) through type_module_compare(), and maps module-trait associations through type_module_trait().
Given a background universe of N total features, module M_1 from Condition 1 containing |M_1| features, and module M_2 from Condition 2 containing |M_2| features, the overlap count is k = |M_1 \cap M_2|.

13.1 Architecture and Coordinate System
cliomicplot provides a composable Grammar of Graphics layer system to couple central modular co-occurrence networks with peripheral multi-domain correlation heatmaps.
The layout operates on a unified Cartesian coordinate system centered at (0, 0) spanning [-7.4, 7.4] on both axes:

title: 13  Central Networks Coupled with Multi-Domain Environmental Heatmaps
text:
Central Network Ring (r \le 2.80): Contains modular network nodes, intra-module edge connections, cluster hulls, and radial module badges.
Annular Link Corridor (2.80 < r < 4.0): Separates the central network perimeter from the peripheral heatmaps. Outer boundary dots mark r \approx 3.38.
Corner Triangular Heatmaps: Four triangular correlation heatmaps occupy the corners. Diagonal indicator points connect via curved segments to central modules.
Inter-Domain Links: Curved lines originate from peripheral indicators and connect to central module perimeters. Line width scales with statistical significance (-\log_{10}P), and color denotes correlation direction.

title: 13  Central Networks Coupled with Multi-Domain Environmental Heatmaps
text:
13.2 Layered Grammar of Graphics
The grammar separates coordinate computation from geometry rendering:

cli_env_network_data(): Computes spatial layouts, node positions, intra-module edges, cluster convex hulls, triangular heatmap coordinates, and link trajectories. Returns an S3 object of class cli_env_network_data.
geom_env_boundary(): Draws the circular boundary ring at r = 2.80 and the outer concentric dots at r \approx 3.38.
geom_env_central_network(): Draws central intra-module edges, cluster convex hulls, node glyphs (shape 16 fill-only), and module label badges.
geom_env_corner_heatmaps(): Draws triangular correlation tiles, significance asterisks or correlation values, diagonal connector points, 78° angled variable labels, and domain titles.
geom_env_links(): Draws curved inter-domain connecting lines weighted by significance and direction.
coord_env_network(): Enforces a 1:1 circular aspect ratio with standard viewport boundaries (xlim = c(-7.4, 7.4), ylim = c(-7.4, 7.4)).
theme_env_network(): Removes Cartesian grid lines and axis ticks while positioning a multi-tier publication legend.


13.2.1 Composing with the + Operator


Show R code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Generate grammatical data object
d <- cli_env_network_data(preset = "nature", show_values = TRUE)

# 2. Assemble plot layer by layer
p_grammar <- ggplot() +
  geom_env_boundary(data = d) +
  geom_env_central_network(data = d) +
  geom_env_corner_heatmaps(data = d) +
  geom_env_links(data = d) +
  coord_env_network() +
  theme_env_network(preset = "nature") +
  labs(title = "Layer-by-Layer Grammar Assembly (Nature Preset)")

  p <- length(vars)
  m <- matrix(runif(p * p, 0.2, 0.8), p, p)
  diag(m) <- 1.0
  m[lower.tri(m)] <- t(m)[lower.tri(m)]
  dimnames(m) <- list(vars, vars)

}

  "Climate"     = make_cor(c("Temp", "Rainfall", "Humidity"))
)

text:
14.1 Module Preservation Statistics (Z_{\text{summary}})
Assessing biological network changes between health and disease requires testing whether module structures persist and whether the network withstands random loss or targeted hub disruption.
cli_module_preservation() evaluates whether module density and intramodular hub rank are preserved between reference and test conditions under permutation testing (Langfelder et al., PLoS Comput Biol 2011).
crumbs: Part IV — Systems Biology and Coupled Multi-Network Architectures
14  Module Preservation and Targeted Attack Robustness

title: 14  Module Preservation and Targeted Attack Robustness
text:
14.1.1 Mathematical Definition of Z_{\text{summary}}
The composite preservation statistic Z_{\text{summary}} aggregates density and connectivity preservation metrics over B permutations:
Z_{\text{summary}} = \frac{Z_{\text{density}} + Z_{\text{connectivity}}}{2}
where Z_{\text{density}} evaluates whether features within module q maintain elevated mutual correlation and clustering in the test condition:
Z_{\text{density}} = \frac{Z_{\text{mean\_adj}} + Z_{\text{mean\_k}} + Z_{\text{cluster\_coef}} + Z_{\text{density\_raw}}}{4}
and Z_{\text{connectivity}} evaluates whether intramodular hub feature rankings are conserved between reference and test networks:
Z_{\text{connectivity}} = \frac{Z_{\text{kIM}} + Z_{\text{kME}}}{2}, \quad Z = \frac{\text{obs} - \mu_{\text{perm}}}{\sigma_{\text{perm}}}

Preservation Thresholds:

Z < 2 (dashed red line): No statistical evidence of module preservation.
2 \le Z \le 10 (dashed orange line): Moderate module preservation.
Z > 10 (dashed green line): Strong, statistically significant module preservation.

demo_omics <- cli_demo_vitality_multiomics(n_samples = 35, n_features = 60, seed = 42)

pres_stats <- cli_module_preservation(
  ref_data    = demo_omics$ref_expr,
  test_data   = demo_omics$test_expr,
  ref_modules = demo_omics$modules,
  n_perm      = 100,
  seed        = 42
)

cliplot_module_preservation(
  pres_stats,
  title = "Cross-Network Module Preservation: WT Reference vs KO Test"
)

text:
14.2 Network Robustness and Targeted Attack Simulation
cli_network_robustness() simulates progressive network degradation under random node loss versus targeted attacks on high-degree hub nodes. cliplot_network_robustness() displays natural connectivity decay curves.

14.2.1 Mathematical Formulation of Natural Connectivity
Natural connectivity \bar{\lambda} derives from the spectrum of the network adjacency matrix A and reflects the redundancy of alternative paths between all node pairs (Wu et al., IEEE Trans Reliab 2012):
\bar{\lambda} = \ln \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N e^{\lambda_i} \right)
where \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_N are the eigenvalues of A. Natural connectivity strictly decreases monotonically as edges and nodes are removed, quantifying alternate path redundancy and topological stability.
The competitive-to-cooperative edge balance is evaluated as:
R_{\pm} = \frac{E_{-}}{E_{+}}


Show R code
rob_stats <- cli_network_robustness(
  networks     = demo_omics$networks,
  attack       = c("random", "degree"),
  rm_fractions = seq(0.05, 0.85, by = 0.05),
  n_perm       = 20,
  metric       = "natural_connectivity",
  seed         = 42
)

cliplot_network_robustness(
  rob_stats,
  title = "Network Robustness Under Progressive Node Removal"
)

section: 14.3 Zi-Pi Keystone Ecological Role Plot: type = "zipi"
text:
14.3 Zi-Pi Keystone Ecological Role Plot: type = "zipi"
Keystone taxa play disproportionately vital roles in maintaining community structure. The Zi-Pi classification framework (Guimerà & Amaral, Nature 2005; Deng et al., Science 2012; Tao Wen et al., iMeta 2025) maps within-module connectivity z-score (Z_i) against among-module participation coefficient (P_i):

Within-module connectivity (Z_i): Z_i = \frac{k_{i, s_i} - \bar{k}_{s_i}}{\sigma_{k_{s_i}}} where k_{i, s_i} is the degree of node i inside its own module s_i, \bar{k}_{s_i} is the mean intra-module degree, and \sigma_{k_{s_i}} is the standard deviation.
Participation coefficient (P_i): P_i = 1 - \sum_{s=1}^{N_M} \left( \frac{k_{i, s}}{k_i} \right)^2 where k_{i, s} is the number of links from node i to module s, and k_i is the total degree of node i.

Standard cutoffs (Z = 2.5, P = 0.62) partition the plane into four topological roles: 1. Peripherals (Z_i \le 2.5, P_i \le 0.62): Module specialists with few inter-module links. 2. Connectors (Z_i \le 2.5, P_i > 0.62): Generalists linking distinct modules. 3. Module hubs (Z_i > 2.5, P_i \le 0.62): Highly connected specialists inside their module. 4. Network hubs (Z_i > 2.5, P_i > 0.62): Super-generalists critical to global network integrity.
type_zipi() automates role classification, renders soft shaded background quadrants, adds marginal density rugs, and labels keystone taxa with collision-free text:

  Phylum = sample(c("Bacteroidetes", "Firmicutes", "Actinobacteria", "Proteobacteria"), n_taxa, replace = TRUE),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

section: 15.2 Permutation Hypothesis Testing for Cross-Network Differences: cli_network_permutation()
text:
15.2 Permutation Hypothesis Testing for Cross-Network Differences: cli_network_permutation()
cli_network_permutation() tests whether global topological properties differ between experimental conditions. The function shuffles group assignments B times, re-estimates correlation networks on each permuted sample, and computes two-sided empirical P-values:
P_{\text{perm}} = \frac{1 + \sum_{b=1}^B \mathbb{I}(|\Delta^{(b)}| \ge |\Delta^{\text{obs}}|)}{B + 1}
The tested metrics are edge density, natural connectivity \bar{\lambda}, negative-to-positive edge ratio R_{\pm}, mean degree, and clustering coefficient.


Show R code
# Stack reference and test samples
comm_combined <- rbind(demo_omics$ref_expr, demo_omics$test_expr)
group_combined <- rep(c("Reference_WT", "Perturbed_KO"),
                      c(nrow(demo_omics$ref_expr), nrow(demo_omics$test_expr)))

perm_res <- cli_network_permutation(
  comm_data  = comm_combined,
  group      = group_combined,
  ref_group  = "Reference_WT",
  test_group = "Perturbed_KO",
  cor_method = "spearman",
  cor_cutoff = 0.35,
  p_cutoff   = 0.05,
  n_perm     = 49,
  seed       = 42
)
print(perm_res)

text:
16.1 The Double-Column Layout Standard
In peer-reviewed publications, individual analyses are assembled into unified, multi-panel composite figures. This chapter explains how to construct double-column figures conforming to Nature and Science standards using patchwork.
Leading journals specify standard column widths: - Single-Column: 89.0 mm (3.5 in) - 1.5-Column: 120.0\text{--}140.0 mm (4.7\text{--}5.5 in) - Double-Column: 183.0 mm (7.2 in)
patchwork combines separate ggplot2 instances while aligning plot axes and standardizing panel tags ((a), (b), (c)).
